paper_title: DuplexGen: Adaptive Synthesis of Human-AI Turn-Taking Dialogues

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Turn-taking is a central component of full-duplex interaction. Which turn-taking behaviors are appropriate varies with the scenario, yet current models apply a single norm regardless of context. This limitation originates in their training data: human-human speech corpora capture natural timing phenomena but provide little role grounding or scenario-specific norms, while heuristic or prompted synthesis methods inject turn-taking behaviors without basing them on human preferences. We introduce DuplexGen, a framework for generating dialogues with scenario-adaptive turn-taking by calibrating LLM predictions against a small set of slot-level human preference annotations. In six cooperative and competitive tasks, human turn-taking preferences differ systematically, and DuplexGen aligns substantially more closely with those preferences than uncalibrated prompting or training solely on generic human-human data; a full-duplex model trained on DuplexGen-generated data exhibits distinctive, human-preferred turn-taking behaviors. These results show that human calibration, not corpus scale or prompt design alone, is what allows turn-taking synthesis to be scenario-specific.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Full-duplex language models (Défossez et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2025) support concurrent listening and speaking, offering an alternative to traditional turn-based systems. central component of this setting is turn-taking, the moment-tomoment coordination of who holds the conversational floor (Sacks et al., 1978). Addressing this challenge requires the assistant to make continual decisions throughout the interaction: whether to take, hold, or yield the floor, and whether to acknowledge the user without claiming it (Wang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Veluri et al., 2024). *Equal contribution. 1 Figure 1: Scenario-specific turn-taking behaviors. No single turn-taking strategy is universally appropriate. Conversation analysis has long established that turn-taking behaviors depend on the social context and role structure of an interaction (Sacks et al., 1978; Skantze, 2021). As Figure 1 illustrates, tutor listens patiently and offers brief encouragements while negotiator interjects more readily. Yet current full-duplex language models do not reflect this scenario-sensitivity. This limitation stems from the data used to train such models. Large-scale corpora of recorded human conversations, such as Switchboard (Godfrey et al., 1992), Fisher (Cieri et al., 2004), and Candor (Reece et al., 2023), were built to capture natural turn-taking at scale, at the expense of role and scenario structure: they pair unfamiliar speakers on assigned topics, without defined task roles. An alternative is to synthesize dialogue data with explicit turn-taking actions, either through heuristic rules (Chen et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025b) or prompted large language models (LLMs) (Wang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025). However, the resulting turn-taking behavior is not validated against what humans actually do in the target scenario; LLM-based methods, in particular, inherit turn-taking prior from pretraining (Liao et al., 2025) that has not been calibrated to any specific interactional setting. Consequently, neither human-recorded nor synthetic datasets directly capture scenario-sensitivity. Figure 2: Overview of the DUPLEXGEN framework. (1) Spoken-style dialogue conversion: converting text-based dialogue to spoken-style transcript format. (2) Turn-taking slot identification: identifying potential turn-taking slots within utterances. (3) Slot annotation and calibration: using small set of human and LLM annotations to calibrate turn-taking predictions. (4) Turn-taking dialogue synthesis: applying the calibrated model when generating turn-taking behaviors on target scenarios. We close this gap with DUPLEXGEN, synthesis framework for scenario-adaptive turn-taking dialogue. As illustrated in Figure 2, DUPLEXGEN converts text dialogue into spoken-style dialogue, identifies candidate slots at which listener would plausibly act, and at each slot predicts an action distribution using an LLM calibrated against small set of slot-level human annotations per scenario. These annotations are collected as distributions over [LISTEN], [BACKCHANNEL], and [TAKE_FLOOR] on streaming partial utterances, rather than hard labels on complete continuations. We instantiate DUPLEXGEN on six tasks spanning both cooperative and competitive interaction settings, including tutoring, planning, interview, negotiation, persuasion, and social chat. These tasks cover different goal structures and relational dynamics, allowing us to study how preferred timing changes across scenarios instead of collapsing all turn-taking into single conversational norm. Our experiments support clear story. First, human turn-taking preferences differ systematically across scenarios, confirming that scenario-adaptive modeling is necessary. Second, models calibrated with small amount of slot-level human supervision align with human judgments substantially better than prompt-only generation and models trained only on generic humanhuman conversation data. We also show that full-duplex language model trained on DUPLEXGEN-generated dataset can show distinctive turn-taking behaviors preferred by humans. Together, these findings identify human calibration as the missing ingredient for scenariospecific turn-taking synthesis. Our contributions are as follows. We introduce DUPLEXGEN, synthesis framework that aligns LLM-based turn-taking with scenario-specific human behavior using only small per-scenario annotation budget. We apply DUPLEXGEN to six tasks spanning cooperative (tutoring, planning, interview) and competitive (negotiation, persuasion, social chat) interaction, and show that (1) small-scale calibration enables humanaligned turn-taking dialogue synthesis, and (2) full-duplex model trained on the resulting corpus exhibits scenario-specific turn-taking preferred by humans.

sections.title: Social Behavior
sections.content: Turn-taking is foundational organizing principle of conversation. Classic conversation analysis describes interaction in terms of turn-constructional units and transition-relevance places (Sacks et al., 1978), where listeners anticipate possible completion points and coordinate entry into the floor. Later 2 psycholinguistic work links response timing to incremental comprehension and production (Levinson and Torreira, 2015), arguing that listeners begin preparing their responses before the current speaker has finished. Computational research has modeled turn-taking with acoustic cues, gaze, gesture, and incremental language signals (Ford and Thompson, 1996; Gravano and Hirschberg, 2011; Ekstedt and Skantze, 2020), often with the goal of minimizing latency or predicting turn boundaries. This line of work explains how conversational timing is coordinated, but it does not by itself resolve central question for spoken AI assistants: what kind of listener action is socially appropriate in given scenario? The same partial user utterance may invite silence, backchanneling, or floortaking depending on whether the assistant is acting as tutor, planner, interviewer, or negotiation partner. DUPLEXGEN builds on the turn-taking literature, but focuses on the problem of modeling scenario-dependent turn-taking preferences rather than generic endpoint prediction alone.

sections.title: 2.2 Turn-Taking Dialogue Resources
sections.content: Existing data resources occupy two incomplete extremes. First, generic humanhuman corpora such as Switchboard (Godfrey et al., 1992), Fisher (Cieri et al., 2004), and Candor (Reece et al., 2023) contain natural speech and naturally occurring timing phenomena, but they are not designed around defined task roles, controlled interaction scenarios, or slot-level supervision over listener actions. They are therefore useful sources of conversational realism, but weak supervision for learning scenariospecific turn-taking norms. Second, recent spoken-style dialogue synthesis pipelines, including Duplex-UltraChat (Zhang et al., 2024), Behavior-SD (Lee et al., 2025), and InteractSpeech (Chen et al., 2025), introduce turntaking through prompting, heuristic rules, or TTSbased conversion. These approaches improve controllability and make it easier to generate large amounts of spoken-style dialogue, but they typically do not ground inserted turn-taking behaviors in human preference annotations for the target scenario. As result, they can produce scenarioconditioned turn-taking without demonstrating that the generated behavior is actually aligned with what humans would want from the assistant. DUPLEXGEN is designed to fill this gap. It combines scenario-controlled dialogue synthesis with small set of slot-level human judgments and context-aware calibration step before generation. In this sense, our contribution is not simply another turn-taking dataset, but humancalibrated synthesis framework for producing scenario-appropriate turn-taking behaviors. 2.3 Full-Duplex Models and Evaluation Recent full-duplex speech language models have made simultaneous listening and speaking practical target for spoken dialogue systems. This shift has motivated growing body of benchmarks and evaluation, including FullDuplexBench (Lin et al., 2025a), FD-Bench (Peng et al., 2025), Talking Turns (Arora et al., 2025), and FLEXI (Ge et al., 2025), which measure latency, gap and overlap behavior, barge-in quality, or context-sensitive response behavior in real-time interaction. These works can evaluate spoken dialogue systems, but they do not solve the upstream data generation problem targeted in this work. Benchmark construction often relies on generic speech corpora, black-box judging, or prompted turn-taking decisions rather than explicit human validation of which action is preferred at each candidate slot. Likewise, models trained only on humanhuman corpora may learn general timing regularities without learning the scenario-specific norms that govern human expectations. DUPLEXGEN is complementary to this line of work. Rather than proposing another benchmark, we focus on generating the kind of training data that full-duplex assistants need but current resources do not provide: dialogues whose turn-taking behavior is explicitly calibrated to human preferences in context. This positioning places DUPLEXGEN at the missing corner between generic speech corpora and prompted synthetic dialogue, namely, humancalibrated, scenario-adaptive turn-taking synthesis.

sections.title: 3 DUPLEXGEN Framework
sections.content: We focus on two linguistically expressible turntaking behaviors, floor-taking and backchanneling, because they represent the fundamental dichotomy of listener responses (i.e., actively claiming versus passively acknowledging the conversational floor) and are both expressible in text, making them directly actionable for LLM assistants. Grounded in conversation-analytic theory (Sacks et al., 1978), floor-taking refers to entering at or near transitionrelevance places, including competitive entries like interruptions. Building upon this classification, we further diversify the scenarios to encompass broad range of interactional contexts. As shown in Table 1, we curate six heterogeneous tasks that simulate turn-taking interactions from widely-used textual datasets. For cooperative scenarios, we include Socratic teaching (TEA; guided knowledge discovery), mixed-initiative planning (PLN; collaborative goal completion), and interviewing (INT; structured information elicitation). For competitive scenarios, we include negotiation (NEG; resource allocation under conflict), persuasion (PER; attitude change attempts), and social chat (SOC; peerlike conversation). Together, these six tasks span diverse goal orientations (task-driven, knowledgeseeking, social), initiative structures (system-led, user-led, mixed), and relational dynamics (expertnovice, transactional, peer-like), ensuring that the resulting turn-taking patterns generalize across the breadth of scenarios an AI assistant may encounter.

sections.title: 3.2.1 Spoken-Style Dialogue Conversion
sections.content: We prompt an LLM to convert text-based dialogues into spoken-style format (B.1) by removing textbased elements such as parentheses (Cho et al., 2024) and rephrasing with speech-oriented elements such as disfluencies and filler words. Table 2 shows an example of spoken-style conversion. This process ensures that the generated dialogue is suitable for speech-oriented turn-taking. Hereafter, we refer to UD as the spoken-style utterance. To assess whether the converted spoken-style dialogues resemble natural human conversations, we compare them with the Switchboard corpus (Godfrey et al., 1992). We focus on sequence matching of lexically identifiable features, namely fillers and repetitions. As shown in Table 3, the converted user utterances exhibit human-like speech characteristics, especially in filler usage. Although repetitions are less frequent than in natural speech, we find this acceptable because excessive disfluency could 4 distract from our main focus on turn-taking dynamics. By contrast, the low rate of these features in AI utterances is intentional, as the AI assistant is designed to deliver information clearly. 3.2.2 Turn-Taking Slot Identification Upon obtaining the spoken-style utterance UD, we identify candidate slots for turn-taking actions by analyzing sentence structure and linguistic boundaries. For given dialogue context and spoken-style utterance UD, we employ both heuristic rules (C.1) and LLM (B.2) to identify natural boundaries where turn-taking could occur. These boundaries typically correspond to clause endings, sentence completions, or other linguistic patterns like hesitations and filler words. We empirically set the maximum distance between consecutive turn-taking slots to 8 tokens, which balances annotation granularity against computational cost while roughly corresponding to typical phrase-length units in conversational speech. sections.title:
3.2.3 Scenario-Specific Turn-Taking
Annotation Calibration
sections.content: To align turn-taking decisions with human judgments about which turn-taking actions are acceptable, we employ calibration process that learns from the agreement between human and LLM annotations. For each scenario, we collect small set of turn-taking annotations where humans and LLMs identify appropriate turn-taking actions respectively. Annotation Collection. For each dialogue in the calibration set (see 4.2.1 for details), we collect two types of annotations. First, we obtain human annotations AH = {(lj, aj)}, where each annotation specifies turn-taking location lj within the user utterance and the corresponding action aj {[LISTEN], [BACKCHANNEL], [TAKE_FLOOR]}. Given xlj D, annotators are instructed to identify appropriate turn-taking slots at which the AI can take the turn. To mitigate the retroactive annotation bias (i.e., annotating after seeing the rest of the conversation) discussed in Umair et al. (2024), we present text chunks incrementally, as illustrated in C.4. We recruit 248 English-speaking participants from the United States and the United Kingdom via Prolific1 and provide the guidelines (C.2). Because turn-taking is inherently subjective, each sample is annotated by five participants, allowing human judgments to be treated as distributions rather than single decisions. Second, we collect LLM annotations AL = {(lj, j)} by predicting turn-taking action probabilities for each candidate slot. To address the miscalibration issue of recent reinforcement learningbased LLMs (Tian et al., 2023), we use verbalized confidence scores (i.e., explicitly generated action distributions) to represent confidence in (B.3). Distribution Calibration. Given paired annotations AH and AL, our goal is to learn calibration function fcal that maps the LLMs raw prediction distribution to one better aligned with human judgments. Although context-agnostic post-hoc methods such as temperature scaling can correct global miscalibration with little data, they apply the same transformation across the scenario and dialogue context, limiting their ability to capture the situational nature of turn-taking. We therefore adopt context-aware calibration via LLM fine-tuning, conditioning on the dialogue history c, and partial utterance xlj to produce calibrated predictions. key design choice is the training target. Rather than reducing human annotations for each slot to majority-vote label, we use empirical annotation counts as soft label, defining the target distribution PH (a xlj D, c) by normalizing over the three action classes. This reflects the subjectivity of turn-taking: multiple actions may be appropriate at given slot, and hard label discards information about human disagreement. We therefore train fcal to align its predicted distribution Pcal(a xlj D, c) with this soft target. We qualitatively observe that it overestimates silence and underestimates backchanneling relative to human annotations, suggesting that general-domain conversational data does not capture the scenario-specific turn-taking norms targeted in this work. 4.3 Can Synthesized Dialogues Enable Scenario-Specific Turn-Taking of Full-Duplex Model? We further evaluate whether DUPLEXGEN can translate calibrated turn-taking preferences into effective full-duplex dialogue behavior, beyond merely improving turn-taking prediction. Unlike slot-level prediction in 4.2, full-duplex interaction requires models to realize turn-taking decisions through temporally coordinated speech behavior while maintaining naturalness and adherence to the interaction scenario. We therefore conduct complementary single-turn and multi-turn analyses: the single-turn analysis examines whether models produce scenario-specific turn-taking behaviors during user speech (4.3.2), while the multi-turn dialogue evaluation assesses whether these behaviors remain natural and contextually appropriate throughout an interaction (4.3.3). Together, these evaluations test whether DUPLEXGEN-based synthesized dialogues can induce scenario-specific turn-taking norms that persist in actual spoken interaction.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We address an important challenge of full-duplex interaction: variable turn-taking norms across different scenarios. We introduced DUPLEXGEN that synthesizes scenario-adaptive turn-taking dialogues by calibrating LLM turn-taking predictions against small set of human annotations. Our experiments show that human turn-taking preferences differ systematically across cooperative and competitive scenarios, reflecting scenario-dependent expectations about when agents should hold, yield, or take the turn. We further show that small calibration budget yields substantially better alignment with human judgments than uncalibrated prompt7https://www.mturk.com 8We observe that real-time user simulator APIs, such as gpt-realtime (OpenAI, 2025a), cannot appropriately handle backchannel simulation, as they stop every time the model produces backchannels. We adopt PersonaPlex for this reason. 9 ing or large generic corpora, and that full-duplex model trained on DUPLEXGEN-synthesized data acquires scenario-specific behaviors preferred by humans. Together, these findings identify human calibration as practical and scalable path toward socially appropriate spoken AI.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: We describe limitations of this work and suggest directions for future development. Data Diversity: Training spoken language models requires substantially greater effort than training their text-only counterparts (Cuervo and Marxer, 2024; Lu et al., 2026), and the current DUPLEXGEN-synthesized datasets cover limited range of scenarios and interaction types. Expanding scenario diversity may not only improve generalization across tasks, but also facilitate the acquisition of broader socially appropriate turn-taking behaviors, as discussed in 4.3. Training Sensitivity: Although scenario-specific dialogues synthesized by DUPLEXGEN enable fullduplex models to exhibit targeted turn-taking behaviors, consistent with Abe et al. (2026), we observe that model behavior remains highly sensitive to data and training hyperparameters, including turn-switching latency, pause duration, and learning rate. Developing robust training recipes for inducing appropriate turn-taking behavior therefore represents an important direction for future work. Text-Grounded Supervision: DUPLEXGEN calibrates turn-taking actions from incrementally revealed transcripts and therefore does not directly condition on prosody, pause duration, intonation, speech rate, overlap, or visual cues. Although the downstream listening study evaluates acoustically realized outputs (4.3.3), it does not establish agreement between text-based and audio-conditioned preference judgments. Paired text/audio annotation and multimodal calibration remain important future directions.

sections.title: B DUPLEXGEN Prompts
sections.content: B.1 Prompt: Spoken-Style Conversion ### Role Expert in refining static, polished text transcripts into lifelike, multi-turn spoken interactions. ### Mission Convert formal text dialogues into spoken versions that emulate real-time, natural conversations between user and an AI assistant. Begin with concise checklist (37 bullets) of what you will do; keep items conceptual, not implementation-level. ### Instructions - Rewrite the provided text dialogue with spoken, conversational flow. - Inject the following stylistic elements based on speaker role: - **User:** Use contractions, natural disfluencies (e.g., "um", "uh", "you know"), some self-repair or repetition (e.g., "I, I"), and informal phrasing. - **AI Assistant:** Maintain professional yet approachable tone; use contractions but avoid disfluencies such as "um", "uh". - Ensure the conversation unfolds reactively, not as monologues. - Safeguard all original facts, goals, and speaker personas. - Omit or replace direct name references. If speaker addresses someone by name, delete it or substitute with generic or natural alternative (e.g., no greeting, "hey", or "you"). - Do not use em dashes () anywhere in the output. Use commas or periods instead. ### Output Format Produce ONLY valid JSON array of objects. Each object must have (cid:96)role(cid:96) and (cid:96)content(cid:96) fields. Example Output: [ {"role": "user", "content": "Hi there, um, was wondering if you could help me?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "I'd be happy to help! What's on your mind?"} ] B.2 Prompt: Candidate Turn-Taking Slot Identification # Role and Objective Transform transcript text by inserting '' symbol after every word that signals the end of logical clause, sentence, or complete thought. # Instructions - Analyze the spoken dialogue text and identify the conclusion of each logical clause. - Insert '' symbol immediately after the final word (and punctuation, if present) marking the end of clause, sentence, or complete thought. ## Detailed Rules 14 - If clause ends with punctuation (e.g., period, comma, exclamation mark, or question mark), place the '' directly after the punctuation (do not remove or replace the original punctuation). - Do not remove or alter existing text or punctuation. - Only insert the '' marker as specified; do not add extra output or commentary. ## Error Handling - If the input text is missing or malformed, return an empty string. # Context Input variable: {original_text} (string containing the spoken dialogue transcript). # Output Format Return **only** the marked text string, with '' symbols marking the ends of logical clauses as described. ### Example **Input:** Well, was thinking maybe we can talk later if you have time. **Output:** Well, was thinking maybe we can talk later if you have time. B.3 Prompt: Verbalized Action Estimation We constrain the output to be structured by Pydantic (Colvin et al., 2025). We observe that smaller models often struggle to produce structured probability outputs, though practitioners may mitigate this issue through further fine-tuning. You are asked to annotate the specific action for potential AI turn-taking when user is speaking, based on **what turn-taking behavior users would prefer at that moment**. # Task You will be given: 1) brief scenario description. 2) dialogue context (four previous turns). 3) The user's current streaming utterance. For the next token generation step, estimate probability distribution over the AI assistant's next action at that moment: - **floor_taking**: The assistant interrupts and takes the conversational floor. - **backchannel**: The assistant produces brief continuer/acknowledgement WITHOUT taking the floor (e.g., "mm-hm", "I see", "right"), and the user is expected to keep speaking. - **silence**: The assistant does nothing and keeps listening. # Output requirements - Return valid JSON only. - Output probability distribution over {floor_taking, backchannel, silence}. - Each probability must be number between 0 and 1. - The three probabilities must sum to exactly 1. # Examples ## Case 1: Backchannel in Cooperative Scenario **User**: "Everything was going smoothly," **Annotator (You)**: You judge that brief feedback here will encourage the user to continue speaking with more engagement in cooperative scenario. **Your Action**: backchannel ## Case 2: Take Floor in Competitive Scenario **User**: "But, think it is" **Annotator (You)**: You judge that interrupting here to provide response will make the user perceive the AI as proactive and engaged in competitive scenario. **Your Action**: floor_taking ## Case 3: Take Floor in Cooperative Scenario **User**: "I think made mistake. should have" **Annotator (You)**: You judge that interrupting here to provide gentle response will make the user feel supported and encouraged in cooperative scenario. **Your Action**: floor_taking ## Case 4: Continue in Any Scenarios **User**: "I decided to go to" **Annotator (You)**: You judge that listening silently here is the best way to keep the user engaged in their story. **Your Action**: silence # Input format Scenario description: <scenario description here> Dialogue context: <dialogue context here> User turn: <user turn here> # Output JSON format 15 { } "floor_taking": PROBABILITY_OF_FLOOR_TAKING, "backchannel": PROBABILITY_OF_BACKCHANNEL, "silence": PROBABILITY_OF_SILENCE B.4 Prompt: Dialogue Synthesis The user and assistant simulation prompts share the same framework but differ in role specification and spoken-style constraints. The user prompt encourages conversational realism, allowing fillers, hesitations, and self-repairs to approximate natural human speech. In contrast, the assistant prompt requires concise and fluent responses while explicitly prohibiting disfluencies. These distinctions ensure that simulated user utterances reflect spontaneous conversational behavior, whereas assistant responses remain clear and professional. All other components, including the interruption handling mechanism and output constraints, remain identical across the two prompts. User Turn Prompt ### System Prompt: Spoken Dialogue Simulator **Role:** You are an expert dialogue simulator specialized in converting static text conversations into realistic, multi-turn **spoken interactions**. Your goal is to mirror the nuances of verbal communication, including reactivity, interruptions, and context-dependent responses. Specifically, you should simulate the user's behavior as human. **Input Data:** 1. **Original Full Text Conversation:** complete, polished transcript of text-based interaction. This serves as the "ground truth" for the facts, goals, and personalities of the speakers. 2. **Partial Transcribed Conversation:** The current history of the spoken simulation. This may contain unfinished sentences or fragmented thoughts. **The (cid:96){TOKEN_FT}(cid:96) Mechanism:** The token (cid:96){TOKEN_FT}(cid:96) represents mid-sentence interruption or rapid turn-take. * **Trigger:** When the (cid:96){TOKEN_FT}(cid:96) token appears at the end of speaker's turn, it indicates that the next speaker has started talking **immediately**. * **Constraint:** You must ignore any content from the "Original Full Text" that would have occurred after the (cid:96){TOKEN_FT}(cid:96) token. * **Response Logic:** Your response must be based **only** on the information provided up to that token. If the speaker was cut off mid-thought, you must react to that partial thought naturally (e.g., asking for clarification, finished their sentence, or responding to the fragment). **Guidelines for Spoken Realism:** * **Brief & Reactive:** Spoken turns are generally shorter than text. * **Contextual Awareness:** If the user cuts you off with (cid:96){TOKEN_FT}(cid:96), acknowledge the shift in topic or the immediate needs of the user. * **Prosodic Adaptation:** While you output text, write in way that sounds "spoken"-include natural hesitations, occasional fillers, or more casual syntax compared to the source text. - Use contractions (I'm, don't, can't) - Include light disfluencies when natural (um, uh, you know) - Occasional short self-repairs are okay - Do NOT use em-dashes (); use commas or natural pauses instead * **Faithfulness to Scenario:** Maintain the personas and objectives established in the Original Full Text, but adapt the *delivery* to the real-time flow of the partial transcript. **Output Constraint:** * **Single Turn Only:** Generate **only one single-turn utterance** with plain text (i.e., no JSON, quotes, or markdown). Do not simulate the rest of the conversation or provide multiple turns of dialogue. Your output should end as soon as your specific turn is complete. **Task:** Analyze the provided **Transcribed Conversation**. Identify if the last turn ended with (cid:96){TOKEN_FT}(cid:96). If it did, generate the next logical response based on that specific cutoff point, ensuring your tone aligns with the **Original Full Text Conversation** while respecting the immediacy of the spoken format.

sections.title: C DUPLEXGEN Annotation Details
sections.content: C.1 Heuristics for Turn-Taking Slot Identification Slots are inserted only in user turns; assistant turns receive none. The location after the final user token is not considered slot. The heuristic identification procedure consists of four stages: 1. Candidate Detection. For each token (except the last), slot candidate is placed after the token if any of the following holds: (a) the token ends with clause/sentence punctuation (. , ? ! ;); (b) the token, lowercased and stripped of punctuation, is hesitation marker (e.g., um, uh, umm, uhh, hm, hmm, huh); (c) an LLM (GPT-4.1-mini with temperature 0) marks the token as clause/sentence boundary via prompted insertion. 2. Cluster Thinning. Runs of consecutive candidates (common after stacked disfluencies such as uh, you know, like,) are collapsed: singleton candidate is kept; for run of length 2, only the 2nd, 4th, 6th, . . . candidates are retained. 3. Long-Gap Fallback. Boundaries are scanned left-to-right. Whenever the gap from the previous slot exceeds 8 tokens, additional slots are inserted at intervals of 4 tokens to ensure turn-taking decision point arises in long unbroken stretches. 4. Tail Handling. The same gap rule is applied between the last detected slot and the turn end, with slots inserted up to but not including the final token. C.2 Human Turn-Taking Annotation Guidelines In 3.2.3, we use Prolific9 to recruit 248 English speakers residing in the United States or the United Kingdom. Participants are compensated C2 for completing 20 annotations, which takes approximately 12 minutes. All participants consented to submit their annotation data before starting the process. # Annotation Guidelines Thank you for participating in this study. For example, humans may find proactive AI assistants helpful in Scenario A, but unwelcome in Scenario B. sections.title: D Ablation on Calibration Data
sections.content: To verify that the amount of supervision for calibrated turn-taking prediction is sufficient, we perform data-scaling ablation. For each scenario, we train the predictor using 10% to 100% of the calibration dialogues (i.e., 2 to 20 dialogues per scenario) and evaluate the held-out test KL divergence. Every training fraction below 100% was repeated with eight independent subsampling seeds, and we report the mean and standard deviation. We use 4B model with SWBD+DUPLEXGEN as the turntaking action predictor. The macro-average over all six scenarios is shown in Table 9. The curve across the amount of calibration data shows diminishing returns, while the performance gradually converged. These results indicate that the current calibration set is sufficient.

sections.title: E Model Training Details
sections.content: E.1 Turn-Taking Predictor Training This section details the training setup behind the turn-taking predictors compared in 4.2. PROMPTONLY performs no gradient updates and is described separately at the end of this section. The three trained variants (SWBD-ONLY, DUPLEXGEN-ONLY, and SWBD+DUPLEXGEN) share the same architecture, objective, and optimization setup, differing only in the training corpora used. Architecture. We adopt token-level classification head on top of Qwen3 backbones (Yang et al., 2025). Concretely, we replace the languagemodeling head with linear layer RH3 mapping the final hidden state at each token position to three-way logit over the action set {[LISTEN], [BACKCHANNEL], [TAKE_FLOOR]}. We instantiate the same head for the three model sizes used in the main experiments (1.7B, 4B, 14B parameters). The dialogue context is rendered with the Qwen3 chat template with thinking mode disabled; for each user turn, candidate turn-taking slots are placed at word boundaries identified by the procedure in B.2. Each candidate slot is mapped to the last sub-word token of the corresponding word via the tokenizer offset mapping, and the cross-entropy is taken at those positions only. are categorical SWBD as Objective. The two corpora differ in slot supervision but share the same bound- (i) SWBD. We parse ary candidate scheme. Switchboard-1 dialog-act annotations (Godfrey et al., 1992; Stolcke et al., 2000) into streaming dialogues in which [BACKCHANNEL] markers are inserted into the surrounding speakers transcript and [TAKE_FLOOR] markers are appended to interrupted utterances; remaining boundary candidates are labeled [LISTEN]. Train and test files are partitioned 9:1 by deterministic hash of the filename, yielding 2.4K dialogues for training. (ii) DUPLEXGEN calibration set. For each of the six scenarios (TEA, PLN, INT, NEG, PER, SOC), we collect five-annotator turn-taking judgments on 20 calibration dialogues per scenario (C.2). The vote counts are re-normalized over {[LISTEN], [BACKCHANNEL], [TAKE_FLOOR]} to form soft targets. In both corpora, we expand each user turn into one prefix-based example 21 per boundary candidate, so that each training example contains exactly one supervised slot at the end of truncated user utterance, mirroring the streaming-inference condition. The dialogue context is restricted to the last four turns. Curriculum. The two calibration variants share the same recipe but differ in initialization: SWBD-ONLY. single stage of supervised training on the SWBD corpus (1 epoch). DUPLEXGEN-ONLY. single stage on the perscenario DUPLEXGEN calibration set, trained independently for each scenario from the off-theshelf Qwen3 weights. SWBD+DUPLEXGEN. two-stage curriculum: we first run the SWBD stage above, then continue fine-tuning the resulting LoRA adapter on the per-scenario calibration set. Hyperparameters. We adopt LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) adapters with rank 8 and α = 16. Optimization uses AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) with learning rate 2104, no weight decay, and constant schedule. The SWBD stage trains for 1 epoch with per-device batch size of 16; the DUPLEXGEN stage trains for 1 epoch with the same batch size. Compute. We train Qwen3-1.7B and 4B variants on 248 GB GPUs and the 14B variant on 448 GB GPUs. PROMPT-ONLY Baseline. PROMPT-ONLY performs no gradient updates: at each candidate slot, the off-the-shelf Qwen3 model is queried with the verbalized-estimation prompt in B.3, and the structured probability output is taken as the predicted distribution. E.2 Full-Duplex Model Training This section describes how we obtain PP-DG, PersonaPlex (PP) baseline fine-tuned on synthetic dialogues generated by DUPLEXGEN. We train one checkpoint per scenario from the public PersonaPlex-7B weights (Roy et al., 2026). Text Dialogues and Filtering. For each scenario, we synthesize text dialogues with the DUPLEXGEN pipeline using GPT-4.1-mini (OpenAI, 2025b) for slot identification and Qwen332B (Yang et al., 2025) for dialogue synthesis, with SWBD+DUPLEXGEN as the turn-taking action predictor. We observe that LLM synthesizers occasionally produce role-swap artifacts in which the user-labeled turn speaks in the assistants voice (or vice versa). To remove these, we run GPT-4.1 zero-shot classifier over every synthesized dialogue that returns boolean swap flag along with the offending turn indices, and drop any dialogue marked as swap before TTS. Spoken-Dialogue Rendering. Each kept text dialogue is rendered into ten two-channel speech variants. Within variant, the assistant uses fixed cloning prompt and the user voice is sampled from LibriSpeech (Panayotov et al., 2015) train-clean-100 and train-clean-360, requiring at least 5 of reference audio per speaker; the ten variants of dialogue use distinct LibriSpeech speakers. Assistant speech is generated by Chatterbox-TTS (Resemble AI, 2025) with cumulative voice prompt of up to 10 s, while backchannels are synthesized by ElevenLabs+10. The two channels are mixed using fixed inter-turn gap of 0.16 s, with user-driven interruptions modeled as stochastic 0.64 overlap and backchannels placed via WhisperX (Bain et al., 2023) word-level alignment. Hybrid System Prompt. We follow the PersonaPlex inference convention and condition every training sample on Hybrid System Prompt that concatenates (i) voice prompt drawn from fixed reference speaker, (ii) brief silence spacer (six frames at 12.5 Hz, about 0.5 s), and (iii) scenario-specific persona description rendered into the agents text channel. Loss on the prompt region is masked so the model is not penalized for reproducing its own conditioning prefix. Fine-Tuning Setup. We apply LoRA adapters with rank 32 and scaling 2.0 to the StreamingTransformer blocks of the PersonaPlex backbone, keeping the embedding tables frozen. Adapters are trained with AdamW (β = (0.9, 0.95), weight decay 0.1) at peak learning rate of 1105 under OneCycle schedule with 5% warmup, in bfloat16 with gradient checkpointing and FSDP sharding across GPUs. Each batch contains two 100-second dialogue chunks per device, trained for one epoch over the scenario corpus. To mitigate token-frequency imbalance and improve turn-onset prediction, we apply 100 loss weight to the first audio codebook, while assigning weights of 0.5 and 10https://elevenlabs.io/text-to-speech 1.0 to the text-padding and end-of-text-padding tokens, respectively.
